The paper was accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Microwave Theory and Techniques in March 2017
The frequency range investigated spans 2-18 GHz, covering microwave and millimeter-wave bands
The material database consisted of 22 different nanocomposite formulations with carbon filler concentrations from 0.5 to 3 weight percent
Epoxy resin (Prime 20LV by Gurit) was used as the polymeric matrix for all nanocomposites
Four types of carbon-based reinforcement materials were employed: PANI, GNP, CNF, and MWCNT
Ring-shaped samples had inner diameter of 3 mm and outer diameter of 7 mm for VNA characterization
Approximately 2000 frequency measurement points were collected for each material sample
Magnetic permeability was found to be approximately 1 for all tested materials, allowing it to be treated as unitary in calculations
The PSO algorithm used 400 exploring particles and ran for over 500 iterations per simulation
Each MATLAB simulation required approximately four weeks of computation time on a 64-processor Dell server
Three multilayered structures were designed and experimentally validated (MEAM 1, MEAM 2a/2b, and MEAM 3)
MEAM 1 was designed to mimic an ideal frequency-selective pattern with sharp reflection variations
MEAM 2 solutions targeted the reflection profile of diluted salt water at 0°C
MEAM 3 was designed to reproduce the reflection profile of dry soil in the 2-10 GHz range
Manufacturing tolerances resulted in thickness discrepancies of approximately 0.1 mm in assembled samples
FEM mesh elements were optimized to λ_min/10 where λ_min ≈ 1.6 cm at the highest frequency
The smallest FEM mesh element size was set to approximately 10⁻⁷ m for accurate electromagnetic analysis
CNT and CNF-reinforced composites exhibited significantly greater dielectric losses than GNP-reinforced materials
GNP-reinforced materials had electromagnetic properties similar to unfilled epoxy polymer
The objective function equally weights all frequencies, which can lead to larger deviations at frequency range boundaries
Experimental measurements showed better agreement with simulations at lower frequencies than at higher frequencies
The transmission coefficient decreased with increasing frequency due to skin-depth effects in the multilayer
Current density analysis revealed that electromagnetic absorption was concentrated in middle layers at 10 GHz
At 18 GHz, electromagnetic field penetration was weaker due to impedance mismatch effects
The proposed method extends beyond previous work by enabling reproduction of arbitrary absorption profiles rather than just broadband or frequency-selective structures
